content: Rosa canina, commonly referred to as the Dog Rose, is a species of scrambling rose that is native to Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia. It is a deciduous shrub that typically grows to a height of 1 to 5 meters, although it can sometimes climb higher into the crowns of taller trees. Its stems are equipped with small, sharp, hooked spines that assist the plant in climbing. The leaves are pinnate, consisting of 5 to 7 leaflets. The flowers are usually pale pink but can range in color from deep pink to white. The plant produces red-orange fruits, known as hips, which measure 1.5 to 2 cm in size. The plant is rich in antioxidants and is particularly noted for its high vitamin C content. Its fruit is commonly used to produce syrup, tea, and marmalade. Rosa canina has historically been cultivated or encouraged to grow in the wild for its vitamin C-rich fruit, especially during times of scarcity or wartime. For example, during World War II, its fruit was used to make rose-hip syrup in the United States, and the plant was grown in victory gardens. It continues to grow widely across the United States, including along roadsides and in wet, sandy areas along coastlines. During the Vietnam War, dried Rosa canina was reportedly smoked with tobacco to produce mild hallucinogenic effects and abnormal dreams. Certain forms of Rosa canina are used as rootstocks for grafting or budding cultivated rose varieties. The wild plant is also utilized as a nurse or cover crop and as a stabilizing plant in land reclamation and specialized landscaping projects. While numerous cultivars of Rosa canina exist, few are commonly grown. One notable cultivar, Rosa canina 'Assisiensis,' is unique in being the only thornless Dog Rose. The hips of the plant are also used as a flavoring in the Slovenian soft drink Cockta. Historically, the Dog Rose was a stylized emblem in Medieval European heraldry and remains in use today. It is also the county flower of Hampshire. The name Dog Rose carries a disparaging connotation, implying worthless in comparison to cultivated garden roses. However, according to Howard (1987), the name may have originated from its use in the 18th and 19th centuries to treat bites from rabid dogs. Other traditional folk names for the plant include Rose Briar, Briar Rose, Dogberry, Herb Patience, Sweet Briar, Wild Briar, Witches' Briar, and Briar Hip. In Turkish, the plant is called kuşburnu, which translates to bird nose.
